units: a living culture forms from flour and water left open to the air
yeasts carried in the air settle in the mixture
the baker takes out a portion and tops it up with fresh flour at regular intervals
after a week the culture holds steady
a sour smell shows that the culture is ready to use
the flour is sifted before the warm liquid goes in
the dough is folded over itself between two rests
the fierce heat of the oven sets the structure and colours the outside
the loaf keeps for a week without drying out
text: Leave flour and water in an open bowl and something living begins. Within two or three nights, yeasts drifting through the air settle in the mixture and lift it. From then on the baker keeps the culture fed at regular intervals: a portion is taken out and thrown away, fresh flour goes in to replace it. A week of that and it holds steady, giving off a sharp, sour smell which means it will raise a whole dough. Sift the flour, pour in warm water, work the starter through with a spatula, then knead until the mass turns supple. Let it rest, fold it over itself, let it rest again. In an oven at its fiercest the structure is fixed for good and the crust takes on its colour. Nothing about the method is quick, and yet it yields a close, fragrant loaf that will sit on the board for a week without drying out.

units: an inn worker leaves her pot on faint embers before going up to bed
she meant to lift it off before sunrise
tiredness keeps her from coming back at the hour she intended
the liquid drops by half and the meat falls apart into threads
the cook skims the surface and then tastes what is there
the sauce turns out thick and faintly sweet
low heat held for a long time altered the tissue of the meat
the customers ask for the same dish the next day
the cook repeats the accident on purpose every evening
text: A cook at a roadside inn set her pot over dying embers and went up to bed, sure she would lift it off before sunrise. Tiredness settled the matter for her. She came down long after first light, and found the liquid halved and the meat fallen loose into soft threads. Thinking the dish ruined, she skimmed the surface, tasted from the ladle, and found a sauce that was thick, dark and faintly sweet. Because the heat had stayed low right through the night, the tough tissue had melted instead of tightening. The travellers at her tables asked for the very same thing the following day. Unable to account for what had happened, she chose to repeat it: every evening she banked the fire down and left the pot to look after itself. A recipe born of forgetfulness made the name of the house.

units: lumps form in a sauce while it is cooking
the pan has to come off the heat straight away
leaving the sauce on the heat gives a burnt taste
adding a cold liquid and then whisking hard breaks up most of the lumps
the sudden change of temperature makes the lumps give way
a fine sieve holds back the pieces that are left
you crush what stays behind with the back of a hollow tool
the mixture then goes back over a gentle flame with constant stirring
slackening the flour in something cold keeps it from happening again
text: Your sauce has gone wrong and lumps are bobbing about in it? Don't tip it away, it can be saved. Get the pan off the heat straight away, or the flour will keep catching on the bottom and the whole lot will taste burnt. Splash in a little cold water and whisk hard: the sudden drop in temperature breaks most of the lumps apart. Any stubborn ones that refuse to give can be tipped through a fine sieve, and you crush what stays behind with the back of a ladle. Then back on a gentle flame, and keep stirring all the while, right out to the edges of the pan. Another time, slacken your flour in something cold before it ever meets anything hot. A smooth sauce hangs on that one habit, not on some knack nobody ever taught you. Keep a whisk within reach; it is the tool that rescues supper.

units: two cooking counters stand facing each other in a covered market hall
the first counter cooks everything by dropping it into hot fat
the queue at the first counter moves quickly
the second counter has had its pots simmering since early morning
customers in a hurry go for the quick method
the two counters charge much the same prices
their outgoings fall on different things
the woman who runs the hall notices that the custom swaps sides as the week goes on
neither counter tries to copy the other
text: Under the roof of a covered market, two cooking counters stand opposite one another and argue for opposite methods. On one side everything goes into hot fat: the fierce heat seals the outside in seconds, and the queue never stalls. On the other, a cook has had her pots simmering since first light, and her service moves at a walking pace. Anyone in a rush turns to the fryer; anyone who sits down waits for the pot. The prices sit close together, though the money goes elsewhere, since one counter gets through oil while the other burns energy hour after hour. The woman who runs the hall notices that the custom swaps sides as the week wears on, hurried at the start, patient towards the end. Neither trader shows any wish to copy the other, and the quiet rivalry keeps the hall full.

units: the goods on the stall are sorted by shade
the first group gathers dried roots and curls of bark
the red goods give off a smell that catches at the throat
the green goods are kept at the back of the stall
a stone vessel stands in the middle of the stall
the inside of the vessel is stained by mixtures made long ago
a worn grating tool is used for hard dried nuts
the trader will not sell anything that has already been ground to powder
he says that powder loses its scent within one season
text: On the spice trader's stall the shades are kept in families. The ochres come first of all: dried roots, curls of bark, powders that smell of resin and of warm, dusty wood. The reds follow, harsher by far, catching at the throat as soon as a hand goes anywhere near. The greens hold the back of the stall, crumpled leaves, minute seeds, stems tied into tight bunches. A stone mortar stands in the middle, its pestle laid across at an angle, the inner wall stained by mixtures made long ago. Beside it a worn grater waits for the hard nuts, which the trader will on no account sell ready ground. Powder, he says, goes flat within a season, while the whole seed keeps its soul. Behind him the cloth sacks sag open on brown treasures nobody can name and no customer ever thinks to ask for.

units: cooking once rested on what the cook could sense
measuring probes changed the nature of the trade
each ingredient can now be given a set band of heat
baths of regulated heat came along afterwards
food sealed under vacuum never climbs past the value aimed at
the writer takes this shift to be a gain
those against it read in it a loss of feeling
the writer argues that the device strips out crude error without deciding the seasoning
what the writer fears most is that results will all come out the same
text: For generations on end, cooking was done by guesswork of a skilled kind: a palm held over the embers, an ear tuned to the sizzle, an eye on the colour. Then came measuring probes, and the trade turned into something else. It grew possible to set a narrow band of heat for each ingredient and hold to it without drifting. The same logic led on to baths of regulated heat, where a sealed piece cooks under vacuum and never climbs past the value aimed at. I take that shift to be a gain, whatever is said by those who read in it a loss of feeling. Measuring forbids nobody to taste: the device strips out the crude failure, it does not decide the seasoning. What troubles me a good deal more is the steady pull towards sameness. A flawless result repeated exactly soon manufactures a flawless boredom.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook comes from a line of millers
her father sorted grain in front of her all through her childhood
she could tell one grind from another by touch before she read a recipe
that early familiarity settled the trade she chose
she started as an apprentice in a neighbourhood bakehouse
the hours worked at night built her stamina
an injured wrist took her away from kneading
that accident turned her towards light work
she sifts her flour twice over to get her layered pastry
she will not enlarge her house now that a trade journal has mentioned it
text: Born into a line of millers, the pastry cook of a small guest house inherited an unusual relationship with flour. Her father sorted grain in front of her, so she could tell one grind from another by touch long before she read a recipe. That early familiarity accounts for the trade she chose. She started as an apprentice in a neighbourhood bakehouse, where the demands of night work built her stamina. An injured wrist then took her off the kneading bench, and the accident turned her towards light work, which asks less of the arms. There she found her signature: pale layered pastry whose lightness comes from flour sifted twice over. Her own apprentices remember one rule above all, to weigh the gesture rather than hurry it. Since a trade journal mentioned her house, she has refused to grow.

units: the room wins the visitor over at once
the menu offers a narrow choice
the vegetables come lukewarm although their dish should have kept them hot
the reviewer works out that the plates waited under a source of heat
the main dish is cooked correctly
the sauce has split for having been brought together too early
the fault lies with the way the work is arranged and not with skill
moving the serving bench nearer the stove would do away with the wait
sending out fewer plates at a time would improve the service
the pudding made to order arrives faultless
text: The room wins you over at once, and the menu is short, which usually promises a kitchen that knows its own mind. The trouble starts with the first course. The vegetables come lukewarm in a cast-iron dish that ought to have kept them scalding; plainly they had been standing under a lamp. The main plate confirms the weakness: the cooking is judged well, but the sauce was brought together too early and had already split. The remedy has nothing to do with talent and everything to do with the way the work is arranged. Bring the serving bench nearer the stove, send out fewer plates at a time, and the delay that spoils the kitchen's own effort goes away. The pudding proves the point, made to order and arriving clean, taut, exact. A kitchen this able should not let a meal begin cold.

units: the reader had asked whether the writer eats better since the move
the writer finds the food different without finding it better
her aunt cooked everything in a single pot
she tipped the leavings of the day before into a broth
the flatmate gives every ingredient a tool of its own
at her aunt's the helpings were generous and piping hot
proportions were never argued over there
in the present home they taste and adjust before serving
the writer misses the smell that used to fill the hallway
the writer asks the reader to come and judge for himself
text: You asked whether I am eating any better since the move. Honestly, it is different, not better. At my aunt's everything came out of one pot; she tipped yesterday's leavings into a broth and out came a meal. My flatmate works the other way round, and every ingredient gets its own pan, its own timer, its own seasoning. At hers we ate hot and we ate plenty, and nobody ever argued about proportions or weighed a thing. Here we taste, we adjust, we start again, and supper lands late. I like both, for opposite reasons. One fed you, the other entertains you. What I miss is the smell that filled the hallway the moment I opened her door. This flat smells of clean. Come over one evening and judge for yourself; I promise not to pick the menu, we will decide together in front of the cupboard.

units: the woman who runs a preserving workshop answers questions about the commonest mistakes
she holds that the quality of the seal matters more than the thickness of the glass
a seal used a second time often gives way as things cool
the water has to cover the jars completely while they are being heated
the top of the contents spoils with nothing to show for it if it stands proud
she points out that salt preserves but also hides the faults of poor produce
the foam that rises on fermenting vegetables is no sign of failure
that foam belongs to the start of the process
she will give no general rule about how long things keep
text: We put the commonest mistakes to the woman who runs a preserving workshop. On choosing jars, she answers that the seal matters far more than the thickness of the glass, and that a seal used a second time will often give way as the jar cools. On heating she is firm: the water has to cover the jars completely, or the top of the contents spoils with nothing to show for it. Asked about salt, she qualifies her answer, since it preserves, yet it also hides what is wrong with poor produce. On fermenting vegetables her reply surprises: the foam that rises is no sign of failure, it belongs to the start of the process. On how long things keep she will give no general rule, and sends you back to the smell, the sound of the lid, the look of the liquid. A careful nose, she ends, beats any label.
